lesson.title: One Full Cycle: What the Period of a Waveform Actually Measures
lesson.summary: The period is the time it takes a repeating waveform to complete exactly one cycle, and it is the simple reciprocal of frequency that every AC calculation quietly depends on.
lesson.body:
Every periodic signal, whether it is a sine wave from a wall outlet or a square wave from a digital clock, repeats the exact same pattern over and over. The period, given the symbol T and measured in seconds, is defined as the time it takes to complete exactly one of those repetitions before the pattern starts again identically. If you could freeze a graph of voltage versus time and slide it sideways by one period, it would land perfectly on top of itself.

Period and frequency are reciprocals of each other: T = 1/f, where frequency f is measured in hertz, cycles per second. A signal that completes 60 cycles every second has a period of 1/60 of a second for each individual cycle, and a signal that takes a full 2 seconds to complete one cycle has a very low frequency of 1/2 = 0.5 Hz. The same relationship connects period to angular frequency omega, measured in radians per second, through omega = 2 pi / T, since one full cycle sweeps through 2 pi radians of phase.

Standard household AC power in the United States is generated at a frequency of 60 Hz. Its period is T = 1/f = 1/60 = 0.01667 seconds, or 16.67 milliseconds, for every single cycle. Check this the other way using angular frequency: omega = 2 pi f = 2 pi (60) = 376.99 rad/s, close enough to 377 rad/s that textbooks often round it that way. Recomputing the period from omega gives T = 2 pi / omega = 2 pi / 376.99 = 0.016667 s, the same 16.67 ms found directly from frequency, confirming the two routes agree.

This is not just bookkeeping. European and most of the rest of the world's AC power runs at 50 Hz instead of 60 Hz, giving a period of T = 1/50 = 0.02 s, 20 milliseconds, noticeably longer than the American 16.67 ms. Every downstream AC quantity, peak value, average value, phase angle, impedance at a given frequency, is computed at a specific instant or over a specific window defined relative to T, so getting the period right first is what makes every later calculation in AC analysis line up correctly.

Not all periods come from power lines. A tuning fork or synthesizer generating concert pitch A above middle C oscillates at 440 Hz, giving a period of T = 1/440 = 0.002273 s, about 2.27 milliseconds, roughly 130 times shorter than a single cycle of AC power line hum. That huge range, from millisecond scale audio tones up to periods of minutes or hours for slow environmental signals, is exactly why frequency and period are always quoted with their units rather than assumed.

It is worth being careful about what counts as one cycle. For a sine wave it is the time between two consecutive peaks, or equivalently between two consecutive upward zero crossings, but never the time between a peak and the very next zero crossing, which is only a quarter cycle, T/4. Getting this distinction right avoids a very common factor of two or four error when reading a period directly off an oscilloscope screen.
